analysis.one_liner: Converts federal K-12 education funding into vouchers for private school and homeschooling, and repeals school meal nutrition standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the House Education and Labor Committee with a single cosponsor when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the main federal elementary and secondary education law and replace it with block grants that states must use for vouchers. Parents of any child aged 5 to 17 could take a per-child federal payment toward private school tuition or homeschooling costs, while public schools would keep a portion for enrolled students. A second title, the "No Hungry Kids Act," would erase the 2012 federal nutrition standards for school lunches and breakfasts and bar any calorie maximum or rule against a child eating a lunch packed at home.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents who send their children to private school or homeschool them would receive federal payments covering tuition, fees, transportation, or homeschooling costs, up to a per-child amount set by each state's block grant [S3]. Private schools would gain a new public funding stream through their students [S3]. Public schools would also receive per-child federal money, but without the poverty weighting of current law [S2, S3]. School food operators would gain freedom from the 2012 nutrition standards, including calorie limits [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Parents of any child aged 5 to 17 could elect a federal payment toward private school tuition, fees, and transportation, or toward the cost of homeschooling, with the payment capped at those actual costs.
The bill keeps federal money flowing to public schools for each enrolled child and requires that it supplement, not replace, state and local school funding.

It repeals the 2012 federal nutrition standards for school lunches and breakfasts and amends the school lunch law so the government cannot set a calorie maximum for individual lunches or stop a child from eating a lunch provided by a parent.

It strips the Education Department of authority over elementary and secondary education beyond approving state applications and sending payments, and ends federal program requirements attached to that money.

analysis.who_pays: Repealing the Elementary and Secondary Education Act would end Title I's poverty-targeted funding, so school districts serving low-income students would lose federal dollars that current law steers to them, since block grants would be split evenly per eligible child [S2, S3]. Children would lose guaranteed nutrition standards in school meals, including calorie and menu requirements [S2, S3]. Taxpayers would subsidize tuition for families who would have chosen private school anyway, and any block grant money left unallotted would go to deficit reduction rather than to schools [S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Elementary and Secondary Education Act ends the federal government's targeting of aid to schools in low-income areas; under the bill's block grant formula, each state simply gets a share based on its total number of children, so districts with the poorest students would lose the extra federal support current law directs to them.

Wiping out the 2012 school meal rule removes the nutrition standards — including calorie limits and menu requirements — that apply to the national school lunch and breakfast programs, and the bill goes further to forbid any calorie maximum for individual lunches.

Funding depends entirely on annual appropriations, and the bill directs any leftover block grant money to deficit reduction rather than to schools, so the voucher amounts could shrink or vary year to year.
The bill limits the Education Department to approving applications and making payments, eliminating federal accountability for how states educate disadvantaged children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The voucher payments would be real money for families who want private school or homeschool options, and letting children eat home-packed lunches addresses a genuine parental complaint about the meal rules. But the bill pays for that choice by dismantling the federal education law's promise that extra money follows low-income students, and it throws out school meal nutrition standards wholesale rather than adjusting the parts parents disliked. An honest backer would acknowledge that the families best positioned to use vouchers are those who can already cover most private tuition, while the districts that lose the most are those serving the poorest children.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on January 24, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The bill drew only one cosponsor, a single Republican, in its two years before the Congress ended.
The committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor, and the full action history shows no activity after the initial referral.
The bill expired on January 3, 2021, having never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school districts kept the federal funding structure that steers extra money to low-income students, and the 2012 school meal nutrition standards stayed in force. Private schools and food operators gained nothing because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public schools and existing meal standards

industries.note: Vouchers would create a new public funding stream for private schools, paid for by converting federal education aid that currently targets low-income public schools into flat per-child payments. Families who already attend private school would capture much of the money.

industries.industry: Public school districts, especially those serving low-income students
industries.note: Repealing the Elementary and Secondary Education Act would end poverty-weighted Title I funding and federal accountability, replacing it with an even per-child block grant. Districts with the poorest students would lose the most.

industries.industry: School food service companies and food and beverage processors
industries.note: Repealing the 2012 nutrition standards and barring calorie maximums would free school meal operators from limits on calories and menu content. The cost would fall on children eating the meals.
Parents who homeschool would receive federal payments covering homeschooling costs up to a per-child cap, creating a paying customer base for curriculum and instruction providers.
